newsitem.title: LEBANON: Profits up/down at Lebanon cement company.
newsitem.headline: Profits up/down at Lebanon cement company.

text.p: Lebanon's biggest cement company Societe des Ciments Libanais reported a 20 percent rise in after-tax profits in 1996 to 22.892 billion Lebanese pounds from 19.025 billion pounds in 1995.

But net profit fell 33.5 percent to 14.993 billion pounds from 22.533 billion in 1995 after a 7.899 billion pounds provision for disputed taxes and penalties demanded by the Finance Ministry for 1992 and 1993.
The company, one of four industrials listed on the Beirut Stock Exchange, issued the results on Thursday at its annual shareholders meeting at its headquarters at Chekka, north of Beirut.

The shareholders approved a 37 pounds (2.4 cents) dividend -- down from last year's 48 pounds -- but voted to freeze payment pending resolution of the long-standing 1992 and 1993 tax and penalties issue with the Finance Ministry.

Chairman Thomas Schmidheiny, who is also chairman of parent company Holderbank, said in his report the board opposed paying the tax and penalties and rejected a possible compromise under which up to 90 percent of the sum could be cancelled by the Finance Ministry.
Schmidheiny told the shareholders a matter of principle was involved.

The shareholders voted to give the board discretion to decide when to distribute the dividend. Company officials said after the meeting they expected a decision by the ministry to settle the issue soon.
SCL, which is Lebanon's second biggest non-banking company after Solidere, said 1996 sales fell 6.9 percent by about 125,000 tonnes of cement to 1,660,997 from 1,785,799 tonnes in 1995.
The company's market share fell to 43.6 percent from 44.9 percent in 1995, the annual report said.
Lebanese cement consumption fell 4.2 percent in 1996 to 3,811,000 tonnes but this exceeded local production capacity and 422,000 tonnes of cement and 758,000 tonnes of clinker were imported.
SCL said its clinker output rose 7.9 percent to 1,184,968 tonnes from 1,098,265 in 1995 and it imported 218,000 tonnes.
A company official said a new kiln under construction was due to go into production in July or August and was expected to reduce costs considerably.

The annual report blamed two major events for the drop in Lebanese cement consumption in 1996 -- a 17-day Israeli blitz on Lebanon in April that killed 200 people and five-week long parliamentary elections in the summer.
